profession_name: Airline Pilots, Copilots, and Flight Engineers

daily_reality.summary: Airline pilots operate large aircraft for Part 121 carriers. They conduct preflight checks, coordinate with ATC, navigate complex airspace, monitor systems, and manage crew. Typical schedule: 12-16 flying days/month with layovers, reserve duty, and mandated rest periods.
typical_tasks: Preflight inspections: fuel, weight/balance, cargo, weather, NOTAMs, aircraft condition
Filing and reviewing flight plans with dispatch
Conducting preflight crew briefings on route, weather, duties
Communicating with ATC for clearances, in-flight adjustments, and approaches
Operating aircraft systems during all phases of flight (taxi, takeoff, cruise, descent, landing)
Monitoring avionics, autopilot, and flight management systems
Managing irregular operations: weather diversions, mechanical issues, passenger medical emergencies
Completing post-flight reports and maintenance write-ups
Reserve/standby duty — available on short notice for callout

deadlines.max_duty_period: Up to 16 hours depending on start time and rest
deadlines.minimum_rest: 10 consecutive hours between duty periods (8 hours uninterrupted sleep opportunity)

daily_reality.seasonality: Peak flying during summer travel season (June-August) and holidays (Thanksgiving, Christmas). Junior pilots often assigned less desirable holiday schedules. Winter brings more weather-related disruptions.

regulatory.summary: Heavily regulated by the FAA under 14 CFR Parts 61, 91, 117, and 121. Pilots must hold ATP certificates, First-Class Medical, and maintain currency. Post-2013 FOQ rule raised entry requirements to 1,500 hours. FAA flight/duty time rules (Part 117) manage fatigue.

key_laws.name: 14 CFR Part 121 — Operating Requirements for Domestic, Flag, and Supplemental Operations
key_laws.description: Core regulations for airline operations including crew qualifications, training, and operational procedures

key_laws.name: 14 CFR Part 117 — Flight and Duty Limitations and Rest Requirements
key_laws.description: Fatigue management rules: flight time limits, duty period limits, and mandatory rest

key_laws.name: 14 CFR Part 61 — Certification: Pilots, Flight Instructors, and Ground Instructors
key_laws.description: Pilot certification requirements including ATP certificate, medical certificates

key_laws.name: First Officer Qualification (FOQ) Rule (2013)
key_laws.description: Requires 1,500 hours total time and ATP certificate for Part 121 first officers

requirements: Airline Transport Pilot (ATP) certificate — minimum 1,500 total flight hours (reduced to 1,000 for military, 1,250 for aviation degree graduates)
ATP Certification Training Program (ATP CTP): 30 hours academic + 10 hours simulator
Type rating for specific aircraft (e.g., B737, A320)
Recurrent training and proficiency checks every 6-12 months
Line Oriented Flight Training (LOFT) and simulator evaluations

regulatory.recent_changes: Effective February 2025, FAA requires ATP to be issued only in conjunction with a type rating. FAA updated Advisory Circular AC 91-78A in 2024 officially allowing EFBs for all phases of flight. Ongoing Congressional debate about reducing 1,500-hour requirement.

tools.summary: Modern glass cockpits with integrated avionics suites, Electronic Flight Bags (iPads), and airline-specific dispatch and scheduling systems. EFB market valued at $3B+ in 2025.

primary_tools.name: Electronic Flight Bag (EFB)
primary_tools.description: iPad-based system for charts, performance calculations, weight/balance, NOTAMs, weather. FAA-approved for all flight phases
primary_tools.examples: Jeppesen FliteDeck Pro, Lido mPilot, airline-proprietary apps

primary_tools.name: Flight Management System (FMS)
primary_tools.description: Integrated avionics computer for navigation, performance optimization, and auto-flight programming

primary_tools.name: Avionics Suite (Glass Cockpit)
primary_tools.description: Primary Flight Display (PFD), Navigation Display (ND), Engine Indicating and Crew Alerting System (EICAS/ECAM)
primary_tools.examples: Boeing 737 MAX display suite, Airbus A320neo cockpit, Garmin G5000

primary_tools.name: ACARS (Aircraft Communications Addressing and Reporting System)
primary_tools.description: Digital datalink between aircraft and airline operations center for flight plans, weather updates, gate assignments

primary_tools.name: Crew Scheduling and Bidding Systems
primary_tools.description: Airline-specific systems for monthly bid, schedule management, trip trading
primary_tools.examples: PBS (Preferential Bidding System), airline crew apps

secondary_tools: ForeFlight or Garmin Pilot (personal flight planning)
Union apps: ALPA, APA member portals
pain_points: Outdated crew scheduling systems at some airlines
Inconsistent automation interfaces between aircraft types
Paper-based processes still required in some legacy systems
Complex and fragmented information sources for weather/NOTAMs

terminology.summary: Aviation has an extensive specialized vocabulary driven by safety, radio communication clarity, and international standardization (ICAO). Mix of formal terminology and informal pilot slang.

terms.glass cockpit: Cockpit with electronic digital flight displays instead of analog gauges
terms.squawk: Set a transponder code (e.g., 'squawk 1200' for VFR)
terms.go-around: Abandoned approach; pilot climbs away to re-attempt landing
terms.heavy: Call sign suffix for large aircraft generating significant wake turbulence
terms.deadhead: Traveling as a passenger to reposition for a flight assignment
terms.slam-click: Pilot who goes straight to the hotel room and doesn't socialize during layover
terms.commuter: Pilot who lives in a different city and commutes to their base via airline travel
terms.crashpad: Shared crash-sleeping arrangement near base for commuting pilots
terms.Zulu time: UTC/GMT — universal time reference in aviation
terms.Wilco: Will comply — acknowledged and will take action
terms.NOTAM: Notice to Air Missions — advisories about hazards or changes
terms.METAR: Meteorological Terminal Air Report — current weather observation
terms.TAF: Terminal Aerodrome Forecast — weather forecast for an airport
terms.SIGMET: Significant Meteorological Information — severe weather advisory
terms.SIC: Second in Command — the first officer/copilot
terms.MEL: Minimum Equipment List — items that can be inoperative for dispatch
terms.LOFT: Line Oriented Flight Training — scenario-based simulator training
terms.IOE: Initial Operating Experience — supervised line flying for new pilots
terms.PBS: Preferential Bidding System — monthly schedule bidding
terms.green time: A new pilot's first months at an airline, often on reserve

career_psychology.summary: Seniority-driven career with dramatic pay progression from regional FO ($70-90K) to major airline captain ($350-550K). High entry costs ($80-150K training). Burnout is significant: 40% report high burnout, 54% report depression/anxiety symptoms. Mental health stigma due to FAA medical certification fears.
career_path: Flight training: Private → Instrument → Commercial → Multi-engine → CFI (cost: $80,000-$150,000)
Flight instructor or time-building job (500-1,500 hours)
Regional airline First Officer (1,500+ hours, ATP-CTP, type rating)
Regional airline Captain (2-4 years at regional)
Major airline First Officer (competitive hiring, 3,000-5,000+ hours typical)
Major airline Captain (8-15+ years seniority at major)
fears: Loss of medical certificate ending career
Failing a checkride or proficiency evaluation
Furlough during economic downturn or airline bankruptcy
Mental health disclosure leading to grounding
Age 65 mandatory retirement approaching (loss of identity)
motivation: Love of flying and aviation passion
Structured schedule with significant days off
Camaraderie and shared identity among pilots
burnout_factors: 40% of airline pilots report high burnout levels
Irregular sleep patterns and circadian disruption
Fear of reporting mental health issues (FAA medical consequences)
Junior pilot reserve schedules — unpredictable, lowest priority
Commuting to base adds fatigue and unpaid time

community.summary: Strong professional community centered around ALPA (80,000+ members), APA, and CAPA unions. Active online presence on forums, subreddits, and YouTube aviation channels.

events: EAA AirVenture Oshkosh (annual, largest aviation gathering in the world)

market.summary: Severe pilot shortage projected to peak in 2026 with 24,000 pilot shortfall. Major airlines hiring aggressively: United plans 2,500 pilots in 2026. Salaries at historic highs. Boeing projects 119,000 new pilots needed in North America over next 20 years.

demand_forecast.major_hiring_2025_h1: 2,190 pilots hired at major airlines in first half of 2025

hiring_plans: Delta Air Lines: 1,000+ pilots annually through 2026
United Express regionals: hiring up 36% year-over-year

salary_market.salary_growth: Up to 86% increases at some carriers since 2022

market_trends: Pilot shortage is the dominant market force — driving salary increases
Mandatory retirement at age 65 creating wave of retirements
Regional airlines struggling to retain pilots as majors offer signing bonuses
Congressional debate on reducing 1,500-hour ATP requirement
Flow-through agreements between regional and major carriers increasing
AI and automation discussions in aviation but no near-term pilot replacement expected
